sections.html:
Just south of Indianapolis lies Johnson County, 321.79 square miles in the Indianapolis-Carmel-Anderson metro area. Franklin holds the courthouse, and Greenwood is the biggest city. The population was 115,209 in 2000, 139,654 in 2010 and 161,765 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 174,262 is a 7.7% rise over 2020. Owners live in 72.9% of occupied homes.

Rapid growth puts older houses next to new ones. If yours is dated or damaged, you can compare a fast as-is sale with the expense of updating it to compete with new construction nearby.

The township and taxing district decide which levies reach your bill, so check your own parcel rather than a neighbor's. Three public school corporations serve Greenwood (Greenwood Community, Clark-Pleasant Community and Center Grove Community), and Franklin Community Schools covers nearly all of Franklin. School levies differ by district, even for two houses a few blocks apart.

Franklin has been through floods. Canary Creek, Hurricane Creek and Young's Creek overflowed in 2008 and damaged or destroyed over 100 homes. The city later bought many of those properties and turned them into green space for its parks system.

Cold matters too. New Whiteland recorded Indiana's all-time low, minus 36 degrees Fahrenheit, on January 19, 1994. Tired pipes, an old furnace or a leaky roof can add up to a costly fix before you list. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is lets you skip that work.

Most seller questions end up at one of five county offices, all open Monday through Friday.

OfficePhoneWhat it covers
Assessor(317) 346-4701Assessed values, deductions and appeals
Auditor(317) 346-4310Tax bills, mailing address changes, deduction processing
Treasurer(317) 346-4330Collecting installments
Recorder(317) 346-4385Recording deeds and mortgages
Planning and Zoning(317) 346-4350Zoning and building questions

The county runs a public mapping site at jcmaps.org, which helps when you want to check a parcel's boundaries or neighbors. The Johnson County department directory has current contacts. Taxes are paid in two installments, May and November.

sections.h2: How the 2025 state law changed bills
sections.html:
Homestead deductions were reworked by Senate Enrolled Act 1 of 2025. The standard deduction is $48,000 for taxes payable in 2026, then falls to $40,000 for 2027, $30,000 for 2028, $20,000 for 2029 and $10,000 for 2030, and is gone afterward.

Going the opposite direction, the supplemental deduction climbs from 40% in 2026 to 46% in 2027 and 52% in 2028. There is also a supplemental homestead credit worth the lesser of 10% of the liability or $300, and nobody has to apply for it. What used to be an over-65 deduction is now a credit of up to $150, limited to incomes of $60,000 for a single filer and $70,000 for joint filers, with an application due January 15 of the first year taxes are payable.

Deductions follow the owner who lives there, so a bill can change after a sale. Bills are also capped against gross assessed value at 1% for homesteads, 2% for other residential and farmland, and 3% for everything else. The state's Tax Bill 101 page explains the caps.

Appeals begin with Form 130, filed with the local assessing official, and cover only the current year's assessed value. After an informal conference with the assessor, a denied appeal moves to the county Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals, and from there to the Indiana Board of Tax Review and the Indiana Tax Court.

June 15 is the deadline. It is June 15 of the assessment year if your notice went out before May 1, and June 15 of the bill-mailing year if it came later. The board has 180 days from filing to hold its hearing. You do not need an appraisal, though one helps, along with a recent sale, comparable sales or an offer to buy.

  • Clerical mistakes, a wrong owner, a missing deduction or an incorrect property description are objective errors. They go on page 2 of Form 130 and can reach back three years of assessments.
  • Refunds also call for Form 17-T.
  • Paying last year's assessed amount during an appeal does not trigger a penalty.

Tax that is owed stays attached to the parcel, and closing usually pays it from the sale proceeds. Until then penalties keep building. The state tacks on another 10% of what is unpaid the day after each installment date in later years, and the end of the road is a tax sale.

Every party to the transfer signs a sales disclosure form before the deed reaches the county auditor. It goes to the assessor for review, then the auditor processes it and returns it to the assessor, who holds it five years. Deeds and sale contracts for value are covered, as are forced transfers through foreclosure, divorce, court order or probate.

A simple order of calls saves time. Phone the Treasurer for the balance on your installments, the Assessor if the value or a deduction looks wrong, and the Recorder once the title company asks where the deed will be filed. Keep your latest tax bill, your parcel number and any payoff letters in one folder, because the title company will ask for each of them. Having them ready keeps the closing date from slipping.

Once you have sold, ask the Auditor to send later bills elsewhere. A change-of-mailing-address form works for up to five parcels and can be mailed to 86 W Court St, Franklin, emailed to the auditor or faxed to (317) 736-7021.

Cash buyers price the house in its current state, and the closing agent can generally pay back tax from the proceeds, so you need not clear the balance beforehand. The steps are identical in Greenwood, Franklin or the townships nearby.

  • Tell the buyer the address and condition, plus any back taxes or liens
  • Get a written cash offer, which you may take or turn down
  • Choose a closing date that suits your move or estate timeline
  • Sign at the title company, which files the deed with the Recorder

If a job change or relocation is behind the sale, you probably have a date to meet, and a cash closing can be scheduled around it. Estate sales follow the same path, since probate transfers fall under the sales disclosure rule.

faqs.q: What are the property tax due dates in Johnson County?
faqs.a: Taxes are paid in two installments, May and November. The county auditor or treasurer can confirm the exact dates for the current year.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Johnson County assessment?
faqs.a: Call the Johnson County Assessor at (317) 346-4701 on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. The state's Form 11 page also lists (317) 346-4705 for the county.

faqs.q: Does Johnson County have a tax sale?
faqs.a: Indiana law allows counties to sell parcels with unpaid taxes, and unpaid taxes can lead to one. Call the treasurer at (317) 346-4330 to ask whether a parcel is at risk.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Johnson County house in an estate?
faqs.a: Yes. Probate transfers are among the conveyances covered by Indiana's sales disclosure rule, and a title company can record the deed once the paperwork is in order. Any tax due is usually paid from the proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: What is a sales disclosure form?
faqs.a: It is a state form that all parties to a conveyance sign before the deed is filed with the county auditor. The assessor reviews it first, and the form feeds the sales data the state uses to adjust values.
